claim: A single early-life antibiotic course (1PAT) accelerated type 1 diabetes (T1D) development in male NOD mice.
source: We found that a single early-life antibiotic course (1PAT) accelerated type 1 diabetes (T1D) development in male NOD mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B where Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrates significantly accelerated T1D in 1PAT male mice compared to controls.

claim: The single antibiotic course had deep and persistent effects on the intestinal microbiome.
source: The single course had deep and persistent effects on the intestinal microbiome, leading to altered cecal, hepatic, and serum metabolites.
evidence: Supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data showing significant changes in microbiome composition persisting from P12 to P49 (Figure 2).

claim: The antibiotic exposure elicited sex-specific effects on chromatin states in the ileum and liver.
source: The exposure elicited sex-specific effects on chromatin states in the ileum and liver and perturbed ileal gene expression, altering normal maturational patterns.
evidence: Demonstrated by histone PTM analysis showing differential effects between males and females (Figure 7).

claim: Four taxa were identified as potentially protective against T1D onset: S24-7, Clostridiales, Oscillospira, and Ruminococcus.
source: Microbiome analysis revealed four taxa each that potentially protect against or accelerate T1D onset, that were linked in a network model to specific differences in ileal gene expression.
evidence: ANCOM analysis identified these taxa as significantly under-represented in PAT mice (Figure 2C), and they were consistently under-represented across multiple timepoints and treatment comparisons.

claim: Four taxa were identified as potentially accelerating T1D onset: Enterococcus, Blautia, Enterobacteriaceae, and Akkermansia.
source: Microbiome analysis revealed four taxa each that potentially protect against or accelerate T1D onset, that were linked in a network model to specific differences in ileal gene expression.
evidence: ANCOM analysis showed these taxa were significantly over-represented in PAT mice (Figure 2C), consistently across timepoints and treatment groups.

claim: In control NOD mice, females had higher T1D incidence than males.
source: In both control groups, females had higher T1D incidence than males, as expected (Bao et al., 2002; Livanos et al., 2016; Markle et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier analysis in Figure 1B and is consistent with established literature on NOD mice.

claim: In male NOD mice, both 1PAT and 3PAT exposures significantly accelerated and enhanced T1D rates compared to controls.
source: In males, T1D development in the two control groups was similar, but both antibiotic-exposed groups had significantly accelerated and enhanced T1D rates (Figure 1B); their similarity indicates the sufficiency of the first exposure for the full effect.
evidence: Demonstrated by Kaplan-Meier survival curves showing significant differences (p=0.019 for 1PAT, p=0.002 for 3PAT) in Figure 1B.

claim: In female NOD mice, neither 1PAT nor 3PAT exposure significantly increased T1D rates beyond the high spontaneous rate.
source: In the female controls, the spontaneous T1D rates approached 80%, and neither antibiotic exposure significantly increased the rates.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1B where female control and PAT groups have similar T1D incidence curves.

claim: The median T1D development in 1PAT male mice occurred at P147.
source: That the median T1D development was at P147 provided a prolonged window to understand the intermediary mechanisms.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experimental data, providing context for the study timeline.

claim: By P70, significantly more pancreatic islets showed inflammation in both 1PAT and 3PAT groups compared to controls.
source: Examining the pancreatic islets, at P42, there were no significant differences between the PAT and control groups, but by P70, significantly more islets showed inflammation in both PAT groups than controls (Figure 1C), confirming that the enhanced pathological process was well-advanced by P70.
evidence: Insulitis scoring data shown in Figure 1C demonstrates significant differences in islet inflammation scores between PAT and control groups at P70.

claim: At P42, there were no significant differences in pancreatic islet inflammation between PAT and control groups.
source: Examining the pancreatic islets, at P42, there were no significant differences between the PAT and control groups, but by P70, significantly more islets showed inflammation in both PAT groups than controls (Figure 1C)
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text and supported by insulitis scoring data in Figure 1C.

claim: 1PAT exposure significantly reduced body weight for both male and female mice continuing to P70.
source: 1PAT exposures significantly reduced body weight for both male and female mice continuing to P70 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Body weight measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 demonstrate significant differences at weeks 3-10.

claim: There was no relationship between early-life body weight and risk or timing of T1D development.
source: There was no relationship between early-life body weight and risk or timing of T1D development.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from analysis of the body weight and T1D incidence data.

claim: On P12, two days after 1PAT ended, there were significant changes in the cecal and fecal microbiota persisting until at least P49.
source: On P12, two days after 1PAT ended, there were significant changes in the cecal and fecal microbiota persisting until at least P49 (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: 16S rRNA sequencing data showing significant β-diversity differences and α-diversity suppression across multiple timepoints (Figure 2).

claim: Community structure (β-diversity) markedly differed between controls and both PAT groups.
source: Community structure (β-diversity) markedly differed between controls and both PAT groups (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: UniFrac analysis shown in Figure 2A demonstrates significant clustering differences between control and PAT groups.

claim: In all cecal and fecal samples tested, 1PAT suppressed α-diversity weeks after the exposure ended.
source: In all cecal and fecal samples tested, 1PAT suppressed α-diversity weeks after the exposure ended (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: Phylogenetic diversity measurements shown in Figure 2B demonstrate significantly lower α-diversity in 1PAT groups at P21, P35, and P49.

claim: The single early life antibiotic pulse led to a persistent change in the microbial community.
source: Thus, the single early life pulse led to a persistent change in the microbial community.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the microbiome diversity and composition data showing sustained differences weeks after antibiotic cessation.

claim: 1PAT increased inter-subject microbial heterogeneity in both males and females.
source: 1PAT also increased the inter-subject microbial heterogeneity. Although the composition of the gut microbiomes of control males and females were nearly identical, there were significant differences in microbiome heterogeneity amongst the 1PAT-exposed mice (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: UniFrac distance analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3 demonstrates increased intra-group distances in PAT mice.

claim: In the ileum, PAT and control differed less from each other than in the cecum.
source: In the ileum, PAT and control differed less from each other than in the cecum (Figure 2—figure supplement 4)
evidence: Comparison of β-diversity and α-diversity metrics between ileal and cecal samples shows smaller effect sizes in the ileum.

claim: 3PAT exposure significantly changed fecal microbiota after course 1 (at P21), course 2 (at P35), and course 3 (at P49).
source: Also consistent with the prior observations, we saw significant changes in fecal microbiota after course 1 (at P21), course 2 (at P35), and course 3 (at P49).
evidence: 16S rRNA sequencing data showing significant β-diversity and α-diversity changes at all three timepoints in 3PAT mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).

claim: β-diversity was markedly different between control and 3PAT groups.
source: β-diversity was markedly different between control and 3PAT, and α-diversity was significantly decreased at all three early timepoints (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: UniFrac analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 5 shows distinct clustering of 3PAT samples from controls.

claim: α-diversity was significantly decreased at all three early timepoints (P21, P35, P49) in 3PAT mice.
source: β-diversity was markedly different between control and 3PAT, and α-diversity was significantly decreased at all three early timepoints (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Phylogenetic diversity measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5 demonstrate significantly lower values in 3PAT groups at all timepoints.

claim: Control males and females were nearly identical in inter-subject heterogeneity, but there were significant differences in the 3PAT-exposed mice at all three timepoints.
source: Whereas the control males and females were nearly identical in inter-subject heterogeneity, there were significant differences in the 3PAT-exposed mice at all three timepoints.
evidence: UniFrac distance analysis comparing intra-group and inter-group distances shows increased heterogeneity in 3PAT mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).

claim: There were no significant differences in α-diversity between males and females for either the control or 3PAT mice.
source: There were no significant differences in α-diversity between males and females for either the control or 3PAT mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Statistical analysis of phylogenetic diversity measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: α-diversities were significantly lower in the 1PAT than the 3PAT group in both males and females.
source: Comparing across the 1PAT and 3PAT experiments based on Shannon index analysis, α-diversities were similar in the two control groups, but were significantly lower in the 1PAT than the 3PAT group in both males (Figure 2—figure supplement 7), and in females (data not shown).
evidence: Shannon diversity index comparisons shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7 demonstrate significantly lower diversity in 1PAT compared to 3PAT.

claim: 76 individual taxa were identified across 518 fecal samples at three early time points.
source: In total, across the 518 fecal samples at the three early time points studied, we identified 76 individual taxa.
evidence: This is a summary of the taxonomic analysis performed on the 16S rRNA sequencing data.

claim: Findings in males and females were similar for taxa affected by PAT, as were comparisons of the 1PAT and 3PAT mice with their controls.
source: Using the stringent ANCOM algorithm (Mandal et al., 2015), findings in males and females were similar, as were comparisons of the 1PAT and 3PAT mice with their controls (Figure 2C)
evidence: ANCOM analysis results shown in Figure 2C demonstrate consistent patterns of over- and under-represented taxa across sex and treatment groups.

claim: The major effects of PAT on taxa were conserved across the treatments and both sexes were affected similarly.
source: thus the major effects on taxa were conserved across the treatments and both sexes were affected similarly (Figure 2—figure supplements 3 and 6).
evidence: Comparison of taxonomic changes across different treatment groups and sexes shows consistent patterns (Figure 2C and supplements).

claim: In essentially all of the 12 individual timepoint/group comparisons, the relative abundances of four taxonomic groups (Enterococcus, Blautia, Enterobacteriaceae, and Akkermansia) were significantly over-represented in PAT.
source: In essentially all of the 12 individual timepoint/group comparisons, the relative abundances of four taxonomic groups (Enterococcus, Blautia, Enterobacteriaceae, and Akkermansia) were significantly over-represented in PAT.
evidence: ANCOM analysis across multiple timepoints and treatment groups consistently identified these four taxa as over-represented (Figure 2C).

claim: The relative abundances of four taxa (S24-7, Clostridiales, Oscillospira, and Ruminococcus) were significantly under-represented in ≥ 7 time-point/treatment comparisons between PAT and control.
source: In contrast, the relative abundances of four taxa (S24-7, Clostridiales, Oscillospira, and Ruminococcus) were significantly under-represented in ≥ 7 time-point/treatment comparisons between PAT and control.
evidence: ANCOM analysis consistently identified these taxa as under-represented across multiple comparisons (Figure 2C).

claim: No other representational differences were reproducible across treatment and time, nor were significant differences identified between males and females.
source: No other representational differences were reproducible across treatment and time, nor were significant differences identified between males and females (Figure 2—figure supplements 3 and 6).
evidence: Statistical analysis of taxonomic data across all comparisons identified only the eight taxa mentioned as consistently different.

claim: Mixed effect analysis confirmed the over-represented taxa (Enterococcus, Blautia, Enterobacteriaceae, and Akkermansia) and the under-represented taxa (S24-7 and Ruminococcus) in PAT.
source: Analysis of the mixed effect of time in different groups further confirmed the over-represented taxa (Enterococcus, Blautia, Enterobacteriaceae, and Akkermansia) and the under-represented taxa (S24-7 and Ruminococcus) in PAT, and revealed another under-represented taxon Anaeroplasma.
evidence: Mixed effects modeling was applied to test relative abundance differences over time, confirming ANCOM results and identifying an additional taxon.

claim: Mixed effect analysis revealed Anaeroplasma as an additional under-represented taxon in PAT.
source: Analysis of the mixed effect of time in different groups further confirmed the over-represented taxa (Enterococcus, Blautia, Enterobacteriaceae, and Akkermansia) and the under-represented taxa (S24-7 and Ruminococcus) in PAT, and revealed another under-represented taxon Anaeroplasma.
evidence: Mixed effects modeling identified Anaeroplasma as significantly under-represented in PAT mice.

claim: 1PAT significantly affected metagenomic composition based on Bray-Curtis analysis of 300 metabolic pathways.
source: Based on Bray-Curtis analysis of 300 metabolic pathways identified in the shotgun sequencing results, 1PAT significantly affected metagenomic composition (Figure 2D).
evidence: PCA analysis of metagenomic pathways shown in Figure 2D demonstrates clear separation between 1PAT and control samples.

claim: Of the 131 pathways differentiating 1PAT and control mice, 97% were overrepresented in the 1PAT samples.
source: Notably, of the 131 pathways differentiating 1PAT and control mice, 97% were overrepresented in the 1PAT samples, significantly deviated from chance at both times in both males and females (p<0.001 for each subanalysis) (Figure 2—figure supplements 8 and 9).
evidence: Statistical analysis of metagenomic pathway abundance shows highly significant directional bias toward overrepresentation in PAT.

claim: A cluster of 34 specific pathways was strongly enriched for 1PAT (20/25 samples).
source: In unsupervised hierarchical clustering of the pathways with the highest inter-individual variance, we identified a cluster strongly enriched for 1PAT (20/25 samples), that contains 34 specific pathways (Figure 2—figure supplement 8)
evidence: Hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 8 identifies a distinct cluster of pathways associated with 1PAT.

claim: The 34-pathway cluster includes genes involved in long chain carbohydrate degradation, specific amino acid biosynthesis, and bacterial cell structural components.
source: encoding genes involved in long chain carbohydrate degradation, specific amino acid biosynthesis, and bacterial cell structural components (e.g. peptidoglycan synthesis and maturation) (Figure 2—figure supplement 8).
evidence: Functional annotation of the pathways in the identified cluster reveals these biological functions.

claim: In males, of 50 pathways that differed significantly between 1PAT and control, 22 (44%) were significant at both P21 and P49.
source: In males, of 50 pathways that differed significantly between 1PAT and control, 22 (44%) were significant at both P21 and P49.
evidence: Statistical analysis of metagenomic pathways across timepoints identifies persistent differences.

claim: For females, of 51 significant pathways, only 9 (18%) were shared between P21 and P49.
source: For females, of 51 significant pathways, only 9 (18%) were shared (Figure 2—figure supplement 9 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Statistical analysis shows less temporal consistency in pathway differences for females compared to males.

claim: Of 49 pathways that were significantly differential at P21, 10 (20%) were shared between males and females.
source: Of 49 pathways significant at P21, 10 (20%) were shared between males and females
evidence: Comparison of significantly different pathways between sexes at P21.

claim: At P49, 19 (35%) of 54 significantly differential pathways were shared between males and females.
source: but at P49, 19 (35%) of 54 were shared.
evidence: Comparison of significantly different pathways between sexes at P49 shows increased overlap compared to P21.

claim: At P21, of 39 pathways that were significantly differential in males, 100% were greater in PAT than controls.
source: At P21, of 39 pathways that were significantly differential in males, 100% were greater in PAT than controls.
evidence: Directional analysis of pathway abundance differences shows complete bias toward overrepresentation in PAT males.

claim: In females at P21, 20 pathways were differential, and 95% were greater in PAT than controls.
source: In females, 20 were differential, but 95% were greater in PAT than controls.
evidence: Directional analysis shows similar bias toward overrepresentation in PAT females, though slightly less complete than in males.

claim: There was a marked asymmetry in the pathways in both males and females, with overrepresentation in PAT.
source: Thus, there was a marked asymmetry in the pathways in both males and females, with overrepresentation in PAT
evidence: Statistical analysis shows directional bias in pathway abundance changes rather than balanced up- and down-regulation.

claim: 10 (53%) of the 19 over-represented pathways in females at P21 also were over-represented in males.
source: 10 (53%) of the 19 over-represented pathways in females also were over-represented in males.
evidence: Comparison of pathway lists between sexes identifies shared pathways.

claim: The 10 shared over-represented pathways were related to bacterial biosynthesis of lysine, methionine, and homoserine and to bacterial degradation of rhamnose, aspartate, and inositol.
source: Those 10 pathways were related to bacterial biosynthesis of the amino acids lysine, methionine, and homoserine and related to the bacterial degradation of rhamnose, aspartate, and inositol.
evidence: Functional annotation of the shared pathways identifies these metabolic functions.

claim: Lysine provides one basis for arginine metabolism, which plays important roles in immune regulation.
source: Lysine provides one basis for arginine metabolism, which plays important roles in immune regulation (Peranzoni et al., 2007)
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature about the metabolic and immunological roles of lysine.

claim: Plasma lysine is substantially produced by intestinal microbes.
source: plasma lysine is substantially produced by intestinal microbes (Metges et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature about microbial contribution to host lysine levels.

claim: Homoserine is an essential part of the Gram-negative enteric bacterial quorum-sensing auto-inducer, homoserine lactone.
source: Homoserine is an essential part of the Gram-negative enteric bacterial quorum-sensing auto-inducer, homoserine lactone, which mediates communication between bacteria and could have immunodulatory roles (Gaida et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial quorum sensing cited from the literature.

claim: Up-regulation of intestinal bacterial amino acid pathways by 1PAT could affect intestinal and systemic homeostasis in the pups and may affect subsequent T1D onset.
source: As such, up-regulation of these intestinal bacterial amino acid pathways by 1PAT could affect intestinal and systemic homeostasis in the pups, and may affect subsequent T1D onset.
evidence: This is a speculative inference connecting the observed pathway changes to potential downstream effects on T1D.

claim: Pairwise correlations between 14 fecal metagenomics pathways were significantly different at P21.
source: Pairwise correlations between 14 fecal metagenomics pathways were significantly different at P21 (Figure 2—figure supplement 10)
evidence: Correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 10 identifies significant relationships between pathways.

claim: There is a close and significant correlation between superpathways of sulfate assimilation and cysteine biosynthesis, phospholipid biosynthesis, purine nucleotide salvage, oleate biosynthesis, (saturated) fatty acid elongation, and hexitol fermentation in all male samples at P21.
source: identifying a close and significant correlation between superpathways of sulfate assimilation and cysteine biosynthesis, phospholipid biosynthesis, purine nucleotide salvage, oleate biosynthesis, (saturated) fatty acid elongation, and hexitol fermentation in all male samples at P21 (Figure 2—figure supplement 10A).
evidence: Spearman correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 10A demonstrates significant positive correlations between these pathways.

claim: The majority of pathway correlation relationships remained when considering 1PAT males at P21 independent of controls, but did not reach significance, likely due to the reduced sample size.
source: The majority of these relationships remained when considering 1PAT males at P21 independent of controls, but did not reach significance, likely due to the reduced sample size (Figure 2—figure supplement 10B,C).
evidence: Correlation analysis stratified by treatment group shows similar patterns but with reduced statistical power.

claim: These pathway correlation relationships were not seen in the control-only analysis.
source: These relationships were not seen in the control-only analysis.
evidence: Comparison of correlation patterns between treatment groups shows differences in pathway co-regulation.

claim: 228 BGCs with high rates of within-sample metagenomic coverage were identified.
source: Using an accelerated optimal gapped alignment algorithm, we mapped the metagenomic reads against a BGC database and identified 228 BGCs with high rates of within-sample metagenomic coverage.
evidence: Bioinformatic analysis of metagenomic data against BGC database identified these pathways.

claim: The number of BGCs per sample varied widely.
source: The number of BGCs per sample varied widely (Figure 2—figure supplement 11)
evidence: Histogram in Figure 2—figure supplement 11 shows variation in BGC counts across samples.

claim: The number of BGCs per sample alone did not significantly distinguish 1PAT in male or female mice.
source: and alone did not significantly distinguish 1PAT in male or female mice (p>0.05, Mann Whitney U test).
evidence: Statistical testing of total BGC counts between treatment groups showed no significant difference.

claim: 23 BGCs were significantly enriched in 1PAT male mice at P21.
source: we found 23 BGCs significantly enriched in 1PAT male mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: Fisher's exact test with FDR correction identified these BGCs as significantly more present in 1PAT samples (Figure 2E).

claim: One enriched BGC mapped to a polysaccharide product in the MIBiG database, produced by Enterococcus species.
source: One enriched BGC mapped to a polysaccharide product in the MIBiG database, and is produced by Enterococcus species (Medema et al., 2015; Xu et al., 1998).
evidence: Database annotation and literature citation identify this BGC as an Enterococcus polysaccharide pathway.

claim: 22 uncharacterized BGCs collapsed to three functional units predicted to produce a triscatecholate siderophore biosynthesis pathway member, a siderophore secondary metabolite, and an arylpolyene, all annotated to the family Enterobacteriaceae.
source: Clustering the other 22 uncharacterized BGCs by sequence homology (Rashidi et al., 2018; Shields-Cutler et al., 2018b), collapsed them to three functional units predicted to produce a triscatecholate siderophore biosynthesis pathway member, a siderophore secondary metabolite, and an arylpolyene, all annotated to the family Enterobacteriaceae.
evidence: Sequence homology clustering and functional prediction based on database annotations identifies these BGC products.

claim: PAT has a directional (not substitutional) effect on the metabolite profiles as detected by metagenomic analyses.
source: In total, these studies indicate a directional (not substitutional) effect of PAT on the metabolite profiles as detected by metagenomic analyses
evidence: The consistent overrepresentation of pathways and BGCs in PAT samples indicates directional change rather than functional replacement.

claim: The metagenomic findings are consistent with changes in taxa that were independently identified in the analysis of 16S relative abundances.
source: and are consistent with changes in taxa that were independently identified in the analysis of 16S relative abundances.
evidence: The BGCs enriched in PAT map to Enterococcus and Enterobacteriaceae, which were also identified as over-represented in 16S analysis.

claim: At P23, the 1PAT mice had significantly reduced levels of butyric and propionic acid compared to controls.
source: At P23, the 1PAT mice had significantly reduced levels of butyric and propionic acid (p<0.05 for both) compared to controls (Figure 3A)
evidence: Targeted GC/MS analysis of cecal SCFAs shown in Figure 3A demonstrates significantly lower levels of these two SCFAs.

claim: None of the other SCFAs were significantly different at P23 between 1PAT and control.
source: none of the other SCFAs were significantly different.
evidence: Statistical analysis of SCFA measurements showed no significant differences for acetic, isobutyric, valeric, and isovaleric/methylbutyric acids.

claim: By P42, there no longer were significant differences in any of the tested SCFA.
source: By P42, there no longer were significant differences in any of the tested SCFA (data not shown).
evidence: Statistical analysis of SCFA measurements at P42 showed no significant differences between groups.

claim: Antibiotic exposure reduced two important host-signaling microbial metabolites (butyric and propionic acid) in early life.
source: Thus, antibiotic exposure, by altering the taxonomic and metagenomic composition, reduced two important host-signaling microbial metabolites in early life.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SCFA measurement data and the known signaling roles of these metabolites.

claim: 30 metabolites were significantly different between 1PAT and control in serum.
source: Using samples obtained from P15 to P42, we identified 30 metabolites that were significantly different between 1PAT and control in serum
evidence: GC-TOF-MS metabolomics analysis identified these differential metabolites (Figure 3B and Supplementary file 2).

claim: 12 metabolites were significantly different between 1PAT and control in liver.
source: and 12 in liver (Figure 3B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: GC-TOF-MS metabolomics analysis identified these differential metabolites.

claim: Three metabolites (uracil, citric acid, and isoleucine) were at significantly higher levels in both serum and liver.
source: These included three metabolites (uracil, citric acid, and isoleucine) at significantly higher levels in both serum and liver
evidence: Metabolomics analysis showed these metabolites were elevated in both tissue types in PAT mice (Figure 3B).

claim: Valine was less abundant in hepatic samples from both the P23 and P42 PAT-exposed mice.
source: and a fourth (valine) that was less abundant in hepatic samples from both the P23 and P42 PAT-exposed mice.
evidence: Metabolomics analysis showed valine was decreased in liver at both timepoints in PAT mice (Figure 3B).

claim: The altered amino acid levels are consistent with the metagenomic representation of amino acid biosynthetic pathways.
source: The altered amino acid levels, consistent with the metagenomic representation of amino acid biosynthetic pathways (Supplementary file 1), provide direct evidence that the PAT-altered microbiome produces a metabolic signal that is transduced into the host.
evidence: The correlation between metagenomic pathway changes and host metabolite changes provides evidence of functional connection.

claim: The PAT-altered microbiome produces a metabolic signal that is transduced into the host.
source: provide direct evidence that the PAT-altered microbiome produces a metabolic signal that is transduced into the host.
evidence: The presence of altered metabolites in host tissues (serum and liver) that correspond to altered microbial metabolic pathways provides evidence of microbiome-host metabolic communication.

claim: Ileal gene expression profiles are distinct at a global level between male and female P2 mice.
source: Bray-Curtis analysis of RNA-Seq data indicated that ileal gene expression profiles are distinct at a global level between male and female P2 mice
evidence: PCA analysis of RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 4A demonstrates clear separation between male and female samples at P2.

claim: Ileal gene expression at P2 significantly differed from P12.
source: and significantly differed from P12 (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: PCA analysis shows distinct clustering of P2 vs P12 samples, indicating developmental changes in gene expression.

claim: At P2, approximately 1500 genes comprised the significant sex-specific differences.
source: At P2, we identified the ~1500 genes that comprised the significant sex-specific differences (Figure 4B)
evidence: DESeq2 differential expression analysis identified 1514 genes with significantly different expression between males and females at P2 (Figure 4B).

claim: Sex-specific gene expression differences at P2 include KEGG pathways involved in the mTOR, MAPK, B cell receptor, and T cell receptor signaling.
source: including KEGG pathways involved in the mTOR, MAPK, B cell receptor, and T cell receptor signaling.
evidence: KEGG pathway analysis of the differentially expressed genes identified these signaling pathways as enriched.

claim: Sex-specific differences at post-natal day 2 may provide an important opportunity to better understand the basis of the T1D sex dimorphism in NOD mice before puberty.
source: These sex-specific differences at post-natal day 2, preceding any antibiotic exposure, may provide an important opportunity in future studies to better understand the basis of the T1D sex dimorphism in NOD mice before puberty.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential significance of the P2 sex differences for understanding T1D pathogenesis.

claim: At a global level, ileal gene expression profiles were significantly different between PAT and control in both males and females at P12.
source: At a global level, the expression profiles were significantly different between PAT and control in both males and females (Figure 4A)
evidence: PCA analysis in Figure 4A shows distinct clustering of PAT vs control samples at P12 for both sexes.

claim: By P12, the antibiotic effects on the microbiome were already being transduced into the tissues.
source: thus by P12, the antibiotic effects on the microbiome were already being transduced into the tissues.
evidence: The significant differences in gene expression at P12 (only 2 days after antibiotic cessation) indicate rapid host response to microbiome changes.

claim: In control mice from P2 to P12, several thousand genes significantly changed in expression.
source: As expected with normal development, expression of several thousand genes significantly changed in the control mice from P2 to P12
evidence: DESeq2 analysis identified 7920 genes in males and 6394 in females with significant expression changes during this developmental period (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: In mice receiving PAT between P5-10, approximately 17% of the maturational gene expression differences were lost in males.
source: however, in the mice receiving PAT between P5–10, ~17% of the differences were lost in males
evidence: Comparison of the number of genes maturing from P2 to P12 shows 6565 in PAT males vs 7920 in control males, a 17% reduction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: In mice receiving PAT between P5-10, approximately 21% of the maturational gene expression differences were lost in females.
source: and ~21% in females (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Comparison shows 5017 genes maturing in PAT females vs 6394 in controls, a 21% reduction.

claim: KEGG analysis of P12 male mice highlighted significant changes between PAT and control in cell adhesion molecules, cytokine–cytokine receptor interaction, T cell receptor signaling, B cell receptor signaling, intestinal immune network for IgA production, and leukocyte transendothelial migration.
source: KEGG analysis of the male mice highlighted significant changes between PAT and control in cell adhesion molecules, cytokine–cytokine receptor interaction, T cell receptor signaling, B cell receptor signaling, intestinal immune network for IgA production, and leukocyte transendothelial migration. (Figure 4C).
evidence: KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes identified these immune-related pathways (Figure 4C).

claim: By P23, 1511 ileal genes showed significant differential expression between PAT and control in males.
source: By P23, we found striking differences between males and females; in males, 1511 ileal genes showed significant differential expression between PAT and control
evidence: DESeq2 differential expression analysis identified 1511 genes (518 up-, 993 down-regulated) in males (Figure 4D).

claim: By P23, only 124 ileal genes showed significant differential expression between PAT and control in females.
source: vs. only 124 in females, a 12.2-fold difference (p<0.001) (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: DESeq2 analysis identified 124 genes (55 up-, 69 down-regulated) in females, significantly fewer than in males.

claim: The 12.2-fold difference in number of differentially expressed genes between males and females at P23 is statistically significant (p<0.001).
source: a 12.2-fold difference (p<0.001)
evidence: Statistical comparison of the number of differentially expressed genes between sexes.

claim: In a functional sense, the female ileum had greater resilience against the same microbiological perturbation.
source: Thus, in a functional sense, the female ileum had greater resilience against the same microbiological perturbation (Figure 2—figure supplement 9).
evidence: The much smaller number of genes affected by PAT in females compared to males indicates sex-specific differences in response to microbiome perturbation.

claim: In males at P23, genes with significantly reduced expression included Nos2, Saa1, Runx1, and Muc4.
source: In the males, the genes that had significantly reduced expression included Nos2, Saa1, Runx1, and Muc4, all involving host defenses (see below).
evidence: RNA-Seq analysis identified these genes as significantly down-regulated in PAT males at P23.

claim: By P42, nearly half of the significant differences in males between 1PAT and controls were lost.
source: By P42, nearly half of the significant differences in males between 1PAT and controls were lost
evidence: Comparison of the number of differentially expressed genes at P23 vs P42 shows reduction from 1511 to 817 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).

claim: 32 days after the antibiotic exposure had ended, there remained abnormal expression of hundreds of ileal genes.
source: nevertheless, 32 days after the antibiotic exposure had ended, there remained abnormal expression of hundreds of ileal genes (Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: At P42 (32 days after P10 when antibiotic ended), 817 genes still showed differential expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).

claim: RNA-Seq studies indicated a broad effect of the microbiome changes on the maturation of early-life intestinal gene expression.
source: Thus, RNA-Seq studies indicated a broad effect of the microbiome changes on the maturation of early-life intestinal gene expression
evidence: The large number of genes affected and the disruption of normal developmental gene expression patterns indicate broad effects.

claim: RNA-Seq studies showed asymmetric effects in males and females, consistent with their differential development of accelerated T1D later in life.
source: with asymmetric effects in males and females, consistent with their differential development of accelerated T1D later in life.
evidence: The sex-specific differences in gene expression changes parallel the sex-specific differences in T1D acceleration, suggesting a mechanistic connection.

claim: Bray-Curtis distance matrix analysis indicated strong and directional age-related effects on immune/inflammatory gene expression from P12 to P42.
source: First, Bray-Curtis distance matrix analysis indicated strong and directional age-related effects from P12 to P42 (Figure 5A)
evidence: PCA analysis of NanoString immune gene expression data shows clear temporal progression (Figure 5A).

claim: The period from P12 to P23 was more developmentally dynamic than that from P23 to P42 for immune/inflammatory gene expression.
source: The period from P12 to P23 was more developmentally dynamic than that from P23 to P42, consistent with the broader RNA-Seq findings (Figure 5—figure supplement 1 top panel).
evidence: Comparison of the number of genes with changed expression status between these two time periods shows more changes in the earlier period (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: The number of genes with changed expression status in the 1PAT mice was similar to control.
source: However, although the number of genes with changed expression status in the 1PAT mice was similar to control (Figure 5—figure supplement 1 bottom panel), many of the maturing genes differed.
evidence: Comparison of gene counts shows similar numbers but different identities of genes changing expression.

claim: Many of the maturing genes differed between 1PAT and control mice.
source: many of the maturing genes differed.
evidence: Comparison of gene lists between PAT and control shows different sets of genes undergoing maturational changes.

claim: Five classes of ileal immune expression maturation were defined: genes maturing in Controls (I), in 1PAT (II), resistant to 1PAT (III), altered by 1PAT (IV), or representing PAT-induced dysmaturation (V).
source: As such, we defined five classes of ileal immune expression maturation (Figure 5B), including genes that significantly matured in: (I). Controls; (II). after 1PAT; (III). maturation was resistant to 1PAT; (IV). maturation was altered by 1PAT; or (V). represented a new pattern of 1PAT-induced maturation (dysmaturation).
evidence: This classification system was developed to categorize the different patterns of gene expression maturation observed in the NanoString data (Figure 5B).

claim: This classification strategy may have general utility in interpreting data from global genetic approaches in other models involving developmental perturbations.
source: Such a classification strategy may have general utility in interpreting data from global genetic approaches in other models involving developmental perturbations.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader applicability of the classification approach.

claim: 1PAT affected Toll-Like Receptor (TLR) signaling pathways.
source: Using these individual gene-level expression differences to understand which KEGG pathways were differentially affected by 1PAT permitted identification of important innate pathways, for example, Toll-Like Receptor (TLR) signaling (Figure 5C).
evidence: KEGG pathway analysis of differentially expressed genes identified TLR signaling as significantly affected (Figure 5C).

claim: 1PAT affected NOD-like receptor signaling pathways.
source: analyses also indicated effects, for example, on pathways involved in NOD-like receptor signaling and Th17 cell differentiation (Figure 5—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: KEGG pathway analysis identified NOD-like receptor signaling as significantly affected (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).

claim: 1PAT affected Th17 cell differentiation pathways.
source: analyses also indicated effects, for example, on pathways involved in NOD-like receptor signaling and Th17 cell differentiation (Figure 5—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: KEGG pathway analysis identified Th17 cell differentiation as significantly affected (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).

claim: In PAT mice, expression was reduced for genes encoding four of the five transcription factors regulating the inducible nitric oxide synthase (Nos2).
source: Using qPCR studies to validate the global findings, we found that in the PAT mice, expression was reduced for genes encoding four of the five transcription factors regulating the inducible nitric oxide synthase (Nos2)
evidence: RT-qPCR validation showed reduced expression of Stat1, Nfkb1, Hif1a, and Crebbp in PAT mice (Figure 6A).

claim: In PAT mice, expression of Nos2 itself was reduced.
source: for Nos2 itself
evidence: RT-qPCR showed significantly reduced Nos2 expression in PAT mice at multiple timepoints (Figure 6A).

claim: In PAT mice, expression of Calm3 was reduced.
source: and the related Calm3 (Figure 6A).
evidence: RT-qPCR showed reduced Calm3 expression in PAT mice (Figure 6A).

claim: Runx1, an early life transcription factor, showed reduced expression with PAT.
source: Runx1, an early life transcription factor showed reduced expression with PAT
evidence: RT-qPCR showed significantly reduced Runx1 expression in PAT mice at P12, P15, and P23 (Figure 6B).

claim: Two downstream genes of Runx1 (Foxp3 and Cd3g) involved in the development of adaptive immunity showed reduced expression with PAT.
source: as did two of its downstream genes (Foxp3 and Cd3g) that are involved in the development of adaptive immunity (Figure 6B)
evidence: RT-qPCR showed reduced expression of Foxp3 and Cd3g in PAT mice (Figure 6B).

claim: Effects of PAT on the innate Saa genes were bimodal over time.
source: but effects on the innate Saa genes were bimodal over time (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: RT-qPCR showed increased Saa expression at early timepoints (P12) but decreased or normalized expression at later timepoints (P42) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).

claim: There was marked reduction of expression of the two major genes involved in intestinal mucin synthesis (Muc2 and Muc4).
source: There was marked reduction of expression of the two major genes involved in intestinal mucin synthesis (Muc2 and Muc4) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: RT-qPCR showed significantly reduced expression of both Muc2 and Muc4 in ileum at multiple timepoints in PAT mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Ido1 showed reduced expression with PAT.
source: Ido1, encoding indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase, the key enzyme catalyzing tryptophan catabolism along the kynurenine pathway and having a major role in immune modulation by mediating T-cell inhibition depending on bone marrow stromal cell activation (Meisel et al., 2004; Munn and Mellor, 2013), showed reduced expression with PAT (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: RT-qPCR showed reduced Ido1 expression in PAT mice in both ileum and colon (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).

claim: The RT-qPCR studies confirmed the gradual normalization of most but not all of the candidate genes.
source: The RT-qPCR studies confirmed the gradual normalization of most but not all of the candidate genes (Figure 6A,B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Comparison of gene expression across timepoints shows that some genes return to control levels by P42 while others remain different.

claim: The 1PAT-altered microbiota interferes with immune pathways during a critical developmental window.
source: In total, these studies provide evidence that the 1PAT-altered microbiota interferes with immune pathways during a critical developmental window.
evidence: The persistent effects on immune gene expression during early life (P12-P42) support this conclusion.

claim: 1PAT-reduction of cecal butyric acid confirmed the prior result with 3PAT.
source: Finding 1PAT-reduction of cecal butyric acid confirmed our prior result with 3PAT (Livanos et al., 2016).
evidence: The current SCFA measurements replicate findings from the previous 3PAT study, providing validation.

claim: By inhibiting histone-modifying genes in intestinal cells, SCFAs including butyrate affect epigenetic status and thus gene expression.
source: By inhibiting histone-modifying genes in intestinal cells, SCFAs including butyrate, affect epigenetic status and thus gene expression (Fellows et al., 2018; Schilderink et al., 2013)
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited literature about the mechanism of SCFA effects on gene expression.

claim: The transcriptional analyses provide direct evidence of dysregulation of histone-modifying genes by PAT.
source: the transcriptional analyses we performed provide direct evidence of such dysregulation.
evidence: RNA-Seq data showed altered expression of histone-modifying genes including Asf1b, Mier1, and Mier3 in PAT mice.

claim: Diminished butyrate levels are consistent with the decreased ileal Runx1 and Foxp3 expression observed.
source: Diminished butyrate levels are consistent with the decreased ileal Runx1 and Foxp3 expression that we observed
evidence: The correlation between reduced butyrate and reduced expression of these genes is consistent with known butyrate effects on these genes.

claim: Reduced butyrate could differentially shift T-helper cell maturation away from Treg-cells.
source: which could differentially shift T-helper cell maturation away from Treg-cells (Furusawa et al., 2013; Geuking et al., 2013; Smith et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge from the cited literature about butyrate's role in Treg development.

claim: Antibiotic-induced gut microbiome remodeling reduced intestinal SCFA levels.
source: Our analyses show that antibiotic-induced gut microbiome remodeling reduced intestinal SCFA levels
evidence: SCFA measurements showed significantly reduced butyric and propionic acid in PAT mice (Figure 3A).

claim: Antibiotic-induced gut microbiome remodeling dysregulated histone PTM status.
source: dysregulated histone PTM status
evidence: LC-MS/MS analysis showed significant differences in histone PTM states between PAT and control mice (Figure 7).

claim: Antibiotic-induced gut microbiome remodeling repressed mucin genes.
source: and repressed mucin genes
evidence: RT-qPCR showed significantly reduced Muc2 and Muc4 expression in PAT mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Reduced SCFA levels, dysregulated histone PTM status, and repressed mucin genes all contribute to perturbing innate intestinal immunity development.
source: all of which contribute to perturbing innate intestinal immunity development.
evidence: This is an integrative conclusion connecting the observed molecular changes to the functional outcome of altered immunity.

claim: Butyrate and propionate both increase histone H3 and H4 acetylation and H3 methylation.
source: Since butyrate and propionate both increase histone H3 and H4 acetylation and H3 methylation, affecting the Muc2 promoter and increasing Muc2 mRNA levels (Burger-van Paassen et al., 2009)
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited literature about SCFA effects on histone modifications and mucin gene expression.

claim: The low SCFA levels observed are consistent with the decreased Muc2 expression.
source: the low levels we observed are consistent with the decreased Muc2 expression.
evidence: The correlation between reduced SCFAs and reduced Muc2 expression is consistent with the known mechanism of SCFA regulation of mucin genes.

claim: Antibiotic administration in early life selected for particular intestinal microbial populations, continuing weeks after the antibiotic stopped.
source: Antibiotic administration in early life selected for particular intestinal microbial populations, continuing weeks after the antibiotic stopped, including small groups of significantly over- and under-represented taxa.
evidence: 16S rRNA sequencing data showed persistent changes in microbial composition from P12 to P49, weeks after antibiotic cessation (Figure 2).

claim: Changes in the representation of taxa with highly active metabolism can initiate the primary events in T1D disease enhancement.
source: Changes in the representation of these taxa, especially those predicted to have highly active metabolism and thus host-interaction, can initiate the primary events in the disease enhancement.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the observed taxonomic changes to disease pathogenesis, based on the metabolic activity of the enriched taxa.

claim: The altered microbial populations and their products, including SCFAs, differentially interact with ileal epithelial cells, affecting histone modification and changing gene expression and its normal maturation.
source: The altered microbial populations and their products, including SCFAs, differentially interact with ileal epithelial cells, affecting histone modification, and changing gene expression and its normal maturation.
evidence: This integrates multiple lines of evidence: altered microbiota (Figure 2), reduced SCFAs (Figure 3A), altered histone PTMs (Figure 7), and altered gene expression (Figures 4-6).

claim: The downstream effects on specific innate genes and pathways and the metabolic changes would then influence how adaptive immunity develops.
source: The downstream effects on specific innate genes and pathways and the metabolic changes would then influence how adaptive immunity develops.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the observed innate immune changes to the adaptive immune changes observed in flow cytometry (Figure 8).

claim: The broad cascade of events altering the expression of specific host genes and pathways appears sufficient to trigger and accelerate T1D in males.
source: Together, the broad cascade of events altering the expression of specific host genes and pathways appears sufficient to trigger and accelerate T1D in males.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion integrating all the findings to explain the T1D acceleration phenotype.

claim: These studies contribute to a growing body of evidence on the effects of early life antibiotic exposures in mouse models of disease.
source: These studies contribute to a growing body of evidence on the effects of early life antibiotic exposures in mouse models of disease (Cox et al., 2014; Nobel et al., 2015; Ruiz et al., 2017; Schulfer et al., 2018)
evidence: This places the current work in the context of related literature on antibiotic effects in mouse models.

claim: The findings are consistent with some epidemiologic studies in humans identifying early life antibiotic exposure as a risk factor for T1D development.
source: and are consistent with some (Pflüger et al., 2010; Yallapragada et al., 2015), but not all (Hviid and Svanström, 2009; Kemppainen et al., 2017) epidemiologic studies in humans identifying early life antibiotic exposure as a risk factor for T1D development.
evidence: This compares the mouse model findings to human epidemiological data, noting both supporting and contradictory evidence.

claim: This simplified animal model advances understanding of the mechanisms by which gut microbiome perturbations contribute to the pathogenesis of T1D and to other immune-associated diseases.
source: This simplified animal model, the taxonomic, metagenomic, and metabolic leads we have identified, and the approach and classification system for gene expression maturation advance understanding of the mechanisms by which gut microbiome perturbations contribute to the pathogenesis of T1D and to other immune-associated diseases.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the significance and contributions of the study.

claim: In male NOD mice, three courses of a pulsed (macrolide) antibiotic treatment (3PAT) altered the intestinal microbiota and reduced intestinal lamina propria Th17- and Treg-populations, accelerating T1D development.
source: In male NOD mice, three courses of a pulsed (macrolide) antibiotic treatment (3PAT) altered the intestinal microbiota and reduced intestinal lamina propria Th17- and Treg-populations, accelerating T1D development (Livanos et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a summary of prior published work cited from the literature.

claim: Isolated cecal contents from antibiotic-exposed NOD mice transferred to germ-free recipient mice produced parallel immunological effects.
source: That isolated cecal contents from the antibiotic-exposed NOD mice transferred to germ-free recipient mice produced parallel immunological effects, further supports a causal role of the antibiotic-perturbed microbiota in T1D pathogenesis (Livanos et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a summary of prior published work demonstrating causality through microbiota transfer experiments.

claim: Enhanced T1D induction depended on the antibiotics used.
source: Enhanced T1D induction depended on the antibiotics used (Brown et al., 2016; Candon et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2017)
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple cited studies showing antibiotic-specific effects.

claim: Differences in antibiotic activities influenced overall effects on T1D.
source: suggesting that differences in their activities influenced overall effects.
evidence: This is an inference from the cited studies about why different antibiotics have different effects.

claim: A single early-life PAT course altered the intestinal microbiota and specific intestinal T-cell populations and effectors in C57BL/6 mice.
source: A single early-life PAT course altered the intestinal microbiota and specific intestinal T-cell populations and effectors in C57BL/6 mice
evidence: This is a summary of prior published work in a different mouse strain.

claim: Experiments involving germ-free mice showed that the perturbed microbiota was both necessary and sufficient for the immunological effects of PAT.
source: experiments involving germ-free mice showed that the perturbed microbiota was both necessary and sufficient for the effects (Ruiz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a summary of prior published work demonstrating causality through germ-free mouse experiments.

claim: The extensive early-life effects of the brief antibiotic course on the microbiota initiate a global cascade of effects flowing from the gut lumen via metabolites and specific interactions with host cells that change the developmental program of innate and adaptive immunity, leading to accelerated and enhanced T1D.
source: This work now shows that the extensive early-life effects of the brief antibiotic course on the microbiota initiate a global cascade of effects flowing from the gut lumen via metabolites and specific interactions with host cells that change the developmental program of innate and adaptive immunity, leading to accelerated and enhanced T1D.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, integrating all the findings into a mechanistic model.

claim: PAT has no effect on gene expression in the ileum in the absence of a microbiota.
source: Our prior studies in C57/Bl6 mice that show that PAT has no effect on gene expression in the ileum in the absence of a microbiota (Ruiz et al., 2017) indicate that the ileal gene expression effects we observed in the PAT-exposed mice were due to the microbiota/metagenemic shifts and were not direct antibiotic effects.
evidence: This is a summary of prior published work in germ-free mice demonstrating that the effects are microbiota-dependent.

claim: The ileal gene expression effects observed in the PAT-exposed mice were due to the microbiota/metagenomic shifts and were not direct antibiotic effects.
source: indicate that the ileal gene expression effects we observed in the PAT-exposed mice were due to the microbiota/metagenemic shifts and were not direct antibiotic effects.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the prior germ-free mouse experiments showing no direct antibiotic effects.

claim: The gut microbiome was substantially remodeled by a single early-life PAT exposure, losing diversity without recovery over the entire window relevant to the development of auto-immunity.
source: We now show in NOD mice that the gut microbiome was substantially remodeled by a single early-life PAT exposure, losing diversity without recovery over the entire window relevant to the development of auto-immunity
evidence: 16S rRNA sequencing data showed persistent reduction in α-diversity from P12 to P49 (Figure 2B).

claim: PAT exposure selected for taxa that may be highly metabolically active.
source: and with selection for taxa that may be highly metabolically active.
evidence: Metagenomic analysis showed enrichment of metabolic pathways in PAT mice, and the over-represented taxa are known to be metabolically active.

claim: Reduced diversity of the gut microbiome compromises the ability to control metabolically active opportunistic bacteria.
source: One hypothesis to explain the heightened auto-immunity is that reduced diversity of the gut microbiome compromises the ability to control metabolically active opportunistic bacteria.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the observed effects, based on ecological principles.

claim: Metabolically active opportunistic bacteria might dysregulate early-life immune responses.
source: Such organisms, as represented by the short list we identified (Figures 2C and 7), might dysregulate early-life immune responses.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism connecting the over-represented taxa to immune dysregulation.

claim: The loss of particular beneficial organisms that participate in normal host metabolic and immune maturation might trigger the pathogenic pathway.
source: Alternatively, the loss of particular beneficial organisms that participate in normal host metabolic and immune maturation, for example, through stimulating mucus production, might trigger the pathogenic pathway.
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis based on the under-represented taxa and their known beneficial functions.

claim: The hypotheses of pathobiont enrichment and beneficial organism loss are not exclusive and may be ecologically linked.
source: These hypotheses are not exclusive, and rather may be ecologically linked, as suggested by our network model (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a statement about the relationship between the two proposed mechanisms, supported by the network analysis.

claim: This study revealed a small consortium of pathobionts (Enterococcus, Blautia, and Enterobacteriaceae species) with consistently increased relative abundances in the PAT-exposed male mice that developed accelerated T1D.
source: This study revealed a small consortium of pathobionts (Enterococcus, Blautia, and Enterobacteriaceae species) with consistently increased relative abundances in the PAT-exposed male mice that developed accelerated T1D.
evidence: ANCOM analysis consistently identified these taxa as over-represented across multiple timepoints and treatment groups (Figure 2C).

claim: Akkermansia, a taxon inversely correlated with obesity, inflammation, and metabolic syndrome, is present in increased relative abundance in PAT-exposed male mice.
source: Akkermansia, a taxon that has been inversely correlated with obesity, inflammation, and metabolic syndrome (Cani and de Vos, 2017), also is present in increased relative abundance in PAT-exposed male mice.
evidence: ANCOM analysis identified Akkermansia as over-represented in PAT mice (Figure 2C), which contrasts with its typical beneficial associations.

claim: The significant overrepresentation of Enterococcus, Blautia, Enterobacteriaceae, and Akkermansia in both 1PAT and 3PAT mice confirms their prior disease-association using the same model in a different mouse facility.
source: The significant overrepresentation of these four taxa in both 1PAT and 3PAT mice confirms their prior disease-association using the same model in a different mouse facility (Livanos et al., 2016)
evidence: The replication of these findings across different experiments and facilities provides strong support for their association with disease.

claim: Enterococcus, Blautia, Enterobacteriaceae, and Akkermansia have been linked to pathological processes in other intestinal microbiome studies.
source: and they also have been linked to pathological processes in other intestinal microbiome studies (Hänninen et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2017; Minter et al., 2017)

claim: Enterococcus species secrete products that alter host immune responses through NFkB/TLR pathways.
source: Enterococcus species, common in both the human and murine gut, secrete products that alter host immune responses through NFkB/TLR pathways (Tien et al., 2017)

claim: Enterococcus species perturb other commensals.
source: perturb other commensals (Fisher and Phillips, 2009)
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited literature about Enterococcus effects on microbial ecology.

source: Akkermansia mucinophila, intestinal mucin-degrading bacteria, may modulate host innate immunity (Derrien et al., 2011, 2004)

claim: Akkermansia mucinophila modulates endocannabinoids, affecting inflammation, gut barrier permeability and peptide secretion.

source: Long-term exposure of older female NOD mice to vancomycin identified Akkermansia as a T1D-protective taxon (Hansen et al., 2012), but that experiment differed substantially from ours

source: in our model, an Enterobacteriaceae taxon other than E. coli was induced by 1PAT across P21 to P49

claim: An unclassified Enterobacteriaceae member was the most significantly increased taxon in T1D children compared to healthy controls.
source: consistent with identification of an unclassified Enterobacteriaceae member as the most significantly increased taxon in T1D children compared to healthy controls (Soyucen et al., 2014).

source: Enterobacteriaceae induce innate immune responses via Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) (Tapping et al., 2000; Vasselon and Detmers, 2002)

source: Enhanced TLR responses to the Enterobacteriaceae could propagate immunopathology

source: consistent with microbiota regulating T1D development through MyD88-dependent TLRs (Burrows et al., 2015).

source: Bacterial siderophore and related transition-metal scavenging responses are often associated with pathobiont organisms and activity

source: NRPS family products are broad in structure but include metabolites with demonstrated anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressant activity such as cyclosporin A (Felnagle et al., 2008).

claim: The small pathobiont consortium found to bloom in this study has many requisite features for T1D immunopathogenesis.
source: The small pathobiont consortium found to bloom in this study has many requisite features for T1D immunopathogenesis.
